result.summary: Ulysses reveals himself and shoots Antinous, then Eurymachus, and with Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius slaughters the suitors, helped unseen by Minerva. He spares only the bard Phemius and the herald Medon, then has the disloyal maids cleanse the hall and hang, Melanthius is mutilated, and the house is purified.

scenes.title: Ulysses shoots Antinous and Eurymachus
scenes.summary: Ulysses throws off his rags and kills Antinous. Eurymachus offers compensation, is refused, and is shot dead when he rushes Ulysses.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks his life and his homecoming facing the whole crowd of suitors alone; the suitors face death.

scenes.title: Arming and the fate of Melanthius
scenes.summary: Telemachus kills Amphinomus and fetches armour. Melanthius brings arms to the suitors but is caught, bound and hung from the rafters.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' party risks being overwhelmed once the suitors are armed; Melanthius risks punishment.

scenes.title: Minerva joins the battle
scenes.summary: Minerva, as Mentor, spurs Ulysses, then perches as a swallow and deflects the suitors' spears. Ulysses' side kills many, and her aegis sends the rest fleeing.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses and his three men risk death against six champions among the suitors.

scenes.title: Mercy for the bard and herald
scenes.summary: Ulysses kills the priest Leiodes but spares Phemius and Medon at Telemachus' plea. He then surveys the dead suitors.
scenes.stakes: Leiodes, Phemius and Medon plead for their lives.

scenes.title: Hanging the maids and purifying
scenes.summary: Euryclea names twelve guilty maids, who clean the hall and are hanged. Melanthius is mutilated, and Ulysses purifies the house with sulphur and is greeted by the loyal women.
scenes.stakes: The guilty maids and Melanthius face death; Ulysses seeks to cleanse the house.

alias_notes.explanation: Minerva takes the voice and form of Mentor, and later a swallow.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses reveals himself, naming the suitors' mistaken belief he would never return.
Ulysses restrains Euryclea: it is unholy to vaunt over dead men.
Ulysses rejects compensation and denies any escape.

analysis.text: Justice and retribution: the suitors' abuse of hospitality and the house is punished, with Ulysses framing it as divine doom for disrespecting all men.
The hanging of the maids and mutilation of Melanthius reflect harsh ancient ideas of household loyalty and punishment of disloyal slaves.

legacy.text: The slaughter of the suitors became a model of epic vengeance and homecoming, echoed in later literature such as Joyce's Ulysses and many retellings.

fun_facts.text: Ancient scholars debated the hanging of the maids; the Greek text says they were hanged like birds in a net, a famous simile.

language_notes.text: "Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; Ulysses hopes Apollo, god of archery, will allow him this shot.
"Another mark which no man has yet hit" is grim irony: the first mark was the axe-head test, and the new target is a living man.
"Looked everywhere towards the walls" means they searched for weapons hung on the walls, which Ulysses and Telemachus had secretly removed.
"Substance" means property and wealth, the household goods and livestock the suitors have consumed.
"Head and front of the offending" means the chief cause and leader of the wrongdoing.
"Give us no quarter" means show no mercy or spare no one's life.
"Redoubtable" means formidable, inspiring fear; "bronze-shod" means the spears have bronze points.
The trap door is a small opening in the wall leading outside, which Agelaus hopes could be used to call for help.
"String him close up to the rafters" means hoist him by a rope up to the roof beams, leaving him hanging in pain.
"Vaunt" means to taunt or boast over a defeated person.
Oceanus is the great river encircling the world; dawn was imagined rising from its streams.
"Cloister" here means the covered colonnade or portico of the hall, not a monastery.
"Age-mate" means a person of the same age; Ulysses appeals to long friendship and shared years.
"Hotch-pot" means a pooling of property into a common stock; here the suitors would merge Mentor's goods with Ulysses' estate.
"Requite" means to repay or return a favour.
"Cloister" here means the covered colonnade or hall of the house, not a monastery.
"Let drive" means to hurl weapons; "crown all the harm" means to cap their earlier wrongs with a final one.
"Bit the dust" means fell dead.
The aegis is Minerva's terrifying divine shield or cape, which strikes panic in those who see it.
Catching the knees is the gesture of a suppliant, formally begging for protection; "beseech" means to implore.
The "trap door" is a small opening in the wall of the hall, used as an escape route; the translator's note 174 refers to it.
The "mixing bowl" was a large vessel in which wine was blended with water before serving.
"Lays" are short narrative songs or poems.
"Fallen in your way" means has happened to cross your path while you were killing.
"Substance" here means wealth or property.
"Cloisters" here means the covered colonnade around the court, not a monastery.
"Vaunt" means to boast or exult. Ulysses says gloating over the slain is impious.
"Carding" wool means combing the fibres straight before spinning.
"Cloister" here means the colonnaded part of the house around the courtyard, not a monastery.
"Lie in secret with the suitors" refers to the maids' sexual relations with the suitors, which Ulysses treats as betrayal of the household.
"Not a clean death" means a shameful death. Hanging was considered more degrading than being killed by the sword.
"Sulphur" was burned to fumigate and purify a place after bloodshed.

context_notes.text: Apollo is the god of the bow. The day is also sacred to him, and the contest was held at his festival.
Oxen were a standard measure of wealth in Homeric society, so a fine of twenty oxen each is a large offer.
Amphinomus was one of the more decent suitors, yet he attacks Ulysses here and dies for it.
Melanthius, the goatherd, serves the suitors and has been disloyal and insolent to his master Ulysses.
Laertes is Ulysses' aged father, so the neglected shield shows the old household's arms left to decay.
Minerva (the Greek Athene), goddess of wisdom and war, is Ulysses' divine protector. Mentor is his old friend who guards Ithaca in his absence.
Ulysses devised the wooden horse stratagem by which Troy, Priam's city, was taken.
Ctesippus had earlier thrown an ox foot at Ulysses, who was disguised as a beggar. Eumaeus now repays the insult.
A priest who sacrificed for the suitors would have prayed at their feasts; Ulysses infers that those prayers included wishing him never to return.
The altar of Jove (the Greek Zeus) in the court was where Ulysses' family had sacrificed, so it offered sacred refuge.
Medon is the household herald. He hid under a fresh cow hide, which was thick enough to cover and protect him.
Euryclea is the old nurse who raised Ulysses and Telemachus, and she is in charge of the household women.
Penelope sleeps because Minerva (Greek Athena) put her into a sleep earlier, so she has missed the slaughter.
Melanthius is the goatherd who sided with the suitors and abused Ulysses. His mutilation is punishment for that.

literary_notes.text: The narrator tells us Antinous suspects nothing, and the reader knows the beggar is Ulysses, which heightens the shock of the shot.
Death "hanging over the head" of every suitor announces the slaughter that follows.
Calling the suitors "Dogs" expresses contempt and shamelessness, and it contrasts with the loyal dogs of his household.
The spilled cup and meats, the kicking feet and the closing eyes make Eurymachus's death vivid, and it echoes Antinous's fall.
The nodding horse-hair crest makes Ulysses' armed figure vivid and threatening as he turns from archer to hoplite.
Telemachus openly accepts blame for the open door, showing honesty and growing maturity.
The narrator suddenly addresses Eumaeus directly as "you," giving him special honor and emotional immediacy.
Eumaeus mockingly calls the rafters a "soft bed," saying the opposite of the painful truth.
Minerva's taunting of Ulysses shows her as a demanding patron who tests the hero, goading him by comparing him to his Trojan past.
Minerva's transformation into a perched swallow shows divine watchfulness: she observes and tests the mortals while still controlling the battle.
The fleeing suitors are compared to cattle maddened by gadflies, stressing their helpless, senseless panic.
Vultures swooping on small birds convey the one-sided slaughter; the detail that onlookers enjoy the sport darkens the tone.
Leiodes pleads that he did only good, yet his own role as priest, praying for Ulysses' failure, is used as proof of guilt.
The head rolling in the dust while the man is still speaking is a grim, vivid image of sudden death.
Ulysses' remark that good deeds prosper over evil ones states the poem's moral view of justice and reward.
The suitors are compared to netted fish left gasping on the beach, making their helpless, ignoble end vivid.
Ulysses stained with gore is compared to a lion after devouring an ox, stressing his terrible, predatory power.
Euryclea is checked for rejoicing aloud, though the vengeance itself has just been carried out with great cruelty.
The hanged maids are likened to thrushes or doves caught in a net, making their deaths seem pitiful and helpless.
Ulysses' wish to weep shows tenderness and memory beneath his violent vengeance, complicating his stern image.
